chunks: And with this chain of transmission, from Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā and others, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad, from al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Luʾluʾī, with his chain, he said:
Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: “All water is tahir (ritually pure) until it is known that it is filthy.”

key_terms.الْمَاءُ: water, the substance under legal discussion in rulings of taharah
key_terms.حَتَّى: until, marking the limit of the ruling
key_terms.طَاهِرٌ: ritually pure and suitable in principle for purification use
key_terms.قَذِرٌ: filthy or impure, meaning no longer considered pure
key_terms.كُلُّهُ: all of it, indicating generality and inclusiveness
key_terms.يُعْلَمَ: it is known, indicating certainty rather than mere suspicion

ai.seo_question: Is all water considered ritually pure in Islam unless proven impure?
ai.summary: This hadith establishes a foundational legal ruling in taharah: all water is presumed tahir (ritually pure) unless its impurity becomes known. It expresses the principle of original purity, which is significant in rulings related to wudu (ablution), ghusl (ritual bath), and general ritual purity.
